extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers studying peer review, psychometrics, philosophy of science, journal editors, and science policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality, reliability, and normative appropriateness of peer review processes and of psychometric measures used to evaluate peer review (e.g., interrater reliability). Emphasizes philosophical (Kuhnian) analysis of interpretive disagreement among reviewers and empirical study of variance sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater reliability as a measure of peer review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychometrically oriented researchers construe low interrater reliability measures for expert peer reviewers as damning for the practice of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article critiques reliance on low interrater reliability (e.g., low agreement among reviewers) as definitive evidence against peer review, arguing that such measures can be misleading unless their sources are analysed; interrater reliability should not be taken at face value without considering legitimate sources of disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normatively appropriate disagreement among reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist different forms of normatively appropriate disagreement among reviewers that can account for variance in ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer disagreement can be reasonable when reviewers legitimately interpret and apply evaluative criteria differently; such normative disagreement should be distinguished from arbitrary disagreement before judging peer review as poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive/application variance of evaluative criteria (Kuhnian perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which variance in reviewer ratings can be accounted for by normatively appropriate disagreements about how to interpret and apply evaluative criteria within disciplines during times of normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should examine discipline-specific interpretive practices: reviewers may apply the same criteria differently because of differing theoretical commitments or standards within 'normal science'—this accounts for some disagreement and affects the meaning of reliability metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-cum-philosophical analysis to distinguish reasonable vs arbitrary disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Until empirical-cum-philosophical analyses are done, it remains unclear the extent to which low interrater reliability measures represent reasonable disagreement rather than arbitrary differences between reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should combine empirical methods (e.g., measurement of rating variance, case studies) with philosophical analysis (normative accounts of appropriate judgment) to determine whether disagreement reflects legitimate pluralism or problematic arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability, validity, bias, and generalizability of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Key psychometric and methodological axes for assessing peer-review systems include reliability, validity, bias, and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements to peer review (including for grant applications) should consider all four dimensions: are ratings consistent (reliability), do they measure what they purport to (validity), are systematic biases present (bias), and do findings/generalizations hold across contexts (generalizability)? (Referenced from Marsh et al. 2008.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of masking/blinding on quality of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomized trials have investigated whether masking reviewer or author identities affects the quality of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding (e.g., anonymizing authors) is an empirical intervention whose impact on review quality should be evaluated experimentally; evidence from trials (e.g., JAMA trials) provides guidance on whether blinding improves or alters review outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment between referees' recommendations and editors' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The association between referees’ recommendations and editors’ final decisions is an axis for evaluating the operational role of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should examine how reviewer recommendations influence editorial outcomes and whether that association reflects appropriate aggregation of judgment or systematic divergence (e.g., studies of association and decision-making processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and uniqueness of reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer comments often show diversity and uniqueness in criticisms; this trait is relevant for judging the informative value of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than treating non-identical critiques as failures, evaluation frameworks should consider the informational contribution of diverse critiques and whether unique perspectives improve editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of peer review as a gatekeeping and quality-control mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence for the effectiveness of peer review (i.e., whether peer review improves publication quality or selection) is a central evaluative concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing effectiveness requires outcome studies and controlled evidence; critiques and support in the literature (e.g., trials, meta-analyses) should inform judgments about whether peer review achieves its intended goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and methodological rigor in manuscript assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical review processes and statistical assessment of submitted work are dimensions for evaluating manuscript (and by extension grant) review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and reviewers should attend to statistical adequacy; editorial processes may include specialized statistical review to improve the reliability and validity of judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential editorial and systemic biases (e.g., against replications, prestige effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication and editorial systems can exhibit biases (against replication research, by prestige, by language, by demographics) that affect peer review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of peer review systems should identify and measure such biases and consider procedural reforms (e.g., incentives, masking) to mitigate them; empirical studies and sociological analyses document these phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of chance vs consensus in peer review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some observed consensus or disagreement among reviewers may arise from chance rather than stable shared standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should separate stochastic variability from meaningful agreement; understanding the contribution of chance informs interpretation of interrater statistics and whether editorial processes reliably discriminate quality.
